    * **L1** (closure): for every even `Δm` and every prime `q | 2^Δm−1` with `q < 2^{Δm/3}`, either some `ℓ ∈ S(q,Δm)` has `ord_ℓ(q)` even, or `L(q,Δm)` has no odd multiple in the window.
    * **L2** (corner): the pairs with `S(q,Δm)` small are exactly those with `q^{n1} ∈ {2^k−1, 2^k+1}`‑type maximality, where `log₂ q ≥ k − m2` and the window contains no integer at all.
    
    ## 3. How the search is made complete *without factoring `2^Δm − 1`*
    
    Let `M = ⌊D·log₂10⌋` (`D = 256 ⇒ M = 850`); since `m1 = ⌊log₂ p⌋`, covering `m1 ≤ M` covers every `p < 2^{M+1} ⊇ p < 10^D`. Fix a split `Q` (default `10^8`).
    
    * **Regime A (`q ≤ Q`).** Precompute once the table `{(ℓ, ord_ℓ(2)) : ℓ ≤ Q prime, ord_ℓ(2) ≤ M}` (FLINT `n_primes_t` + `n_factor`). Then for each even `Δm`, the primes `q ≤ Q` dividing `2^Δm−1` are **exactly** the table entries with `ord_ℓ(2) | Δm` — the §5.3 decision procedure, with no factorisation of the Mersenne number. The same list supplies the partial `S(q,Δm)` used by S8/S9 (a subset only weakens the filter, never invalidates it).
    * **Regime B (`q > Q`).** Here the *exponents* are tiny. From `q^{n2} − q^{n1} = 2^{m1} − 2^{m2} =: N` and `n1 ≤ n2−1`:
     `N < q^{n2} ≤ N·q/(q−1) ≤ 1.5N`, and for `n2 ≥ 2` the only integer with that property is `q = ⌈N^{1/n2}⌉`. So each triple `(Δm, m2, n2)` **forces** `q`, and `q > Q` implies `n2 < (m1+1)/log₂Q` (≤ 32 at `D = 256`, `Q = 10^8`), while `q < 2^{Δm/3}` implies `n2 > 3(m1−1)/Δm`. With `m2 ≤ min(k, M−Δm)` this is a few million `n`‑th roots — minutes, not days.
    
    Every solution of the open case with `p < 10^D` is caught by exactly one regime, and both feed the *same* core test of §1–§2.
    
    ---
    
    # Part II — The program
    
    Single translation unit, FLINT for all number theory (`n_primes_t`, `n_factor`, `n_powmod2`, `n_lcm`, `n_remove`, `fmpz_root`, `fmpz_remove`, `fmpz_powm_ui`, `fmpz_val2`, `fmpz_is_prime`), `std::thread` for parallelism. No composite‑`q` reporting, no ruled‑out cases, one funnel.
    
    ```cpp
    /* =====================================================================
       twinrep.cpp —  p = 2^m1 + q^n1 = 2^m2 + q^n2, same prime base q,
                      open case:  A > 1,  Δm even,  Δn odd.
       Exhausts all p < 10^D (default D = 256, i.e. m1 ≤ 850).
    
       Build:
         g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17 -pthread twinrep.cpp -lflint -lmpfr -lgmp -o twinrep
       Run:
         ./twinrep --digits 256 --Q 100000000 --threads 24 --verbose
    
       Structure (see synthesis):
         * a pair (q, Δm) with q | 2^Δm − 1 determines m2 = v2(q−1),
           n1 = v_q(2^Δm−1), A = (2^Δm−1)/q^{n1}; a configuration exists iff
           A·2^{m2}+1 is an odd power of q.  core_test() decides one pair.
         * regime A enumerates q ≤ Q from a precomputed ord_ℓ(2) table;
         * regime B enumerates q > Q as forced n2-th roots of 2^m1 − 2^m2.
       ===================================================================== */
    
    #include <flint/flint.h>
    #include <flint/fmpz.h>
    #include <flint/ulong_extras.h>
    
    #include <cstdio>
    #include <cstdlib>
    #include <cstring>
    #include <cmath>
    #include <string>
    #include <vector>
    #include <thread>
    #include <mutex>
    #include <atomic>
    #include <algorithm>
    #include <chrono>
    
    /* ------------------------------------------------------------------ cfg */
    struct Cfg {
        int      digits  = 256;
        slong    Mmax    = 0;          /* ceiling on m1 = floor(log2 p) */
        ulong    Q       = 100000000UL;/* small/large split for q        */
        int      threads = 0;
        int      verbose = 0;
    };
    static Cfg cfg;
    
    /* ------------------------------------------------------- funnel stages */
    enum {
        ST_PAIR = 0, ST_SIZE, ST_RANGE, ST_MOD3, ST_ORD2, ST_PRIME, ST_UDIV,
        ST_N1PAR, ST_ODDORD, ST_WINDOW, ST_VAL, ST_EXACT, ST_HIT, ST_N
    };
    static const char *STNAME[ST_N] = {
        "pairs (q,dm) examined",
        "S1  q^3 < 2^dm                      (§9.3,§9.4)",
        "S2  m2 = v2(q-1) <= k, m1 <= Mmax    (§5.2,§9.2 E3)",
        "S3  q = 3 or q = 1 mod 3             (§1 = §5.4 at l=3)",
        "S4  q | 2^dm - 1                     (§5.3)",
        "S5  q prime",
        "S6  u | 2^dm - 1, u = odd part q-1   (§8.1,§8.2)",
        "S7  parity of n1 vs q mod 8          (§7.1,§7.2)",
        "S8  ord_l(q) odd for all l in S      (§5.4,§10.2)",
        "S9  odd dn, L | dn, inside window    (§9.5,§10.3)",
        "S10 valuation identity on dn         (§8.3)",
        "S11 exact  A*2^m2 + 1 = q^dn         (§5.3)",
        "S12 p prime and both representations verified"
    };
    
    
    TWO BUCKETING SCHEMES (both useful; not yet ranked).
    
      (A) Bit-band bucketing -- bucket primes by m = floor(log2 p). Within a band,
          k ~ Binomial(m, p_m) with per-position success p_m ~ 1.88/m (falls as 1/m),
          which limits to Poisson(1.88). The GLOBAL k-distribution is the mixture over
          bands plus per-prime rate heterogeneity = a Gamma-mixed Poisson = the
          observed negative-binomial overdispersion. Banding is thus the decomposition
          that explains the overdispersion: it is a family of Poissons, not one.
    
      (B) m_k bucketing (on the partitions table) -- for each representation exponent
          m_k in [1, floor(log2 max_p)], bucket partitions by m_k. Within a bucket,
          q^n = p - 2^{m_k} = 2^{m_k}(2^{j} - 1), where j := log2(p) - m_k indexes the
          size of q^n relative to its 2^{m_k} anchor on a log2 scale. For the top
          position (m_k = floor(log2 p)) j is the mantissa in [0,1); for lower
          positions j > 1. So j is the log-coordinate of q^n, and binning by j with a
          prime-power-density weight 1/ln(q^n) gives a principled, non-uniform
          per-position hit probability (replacing the uniform 1.88/m). Directly
          checkable against the stored (q, n).
    
    HOW THIS FEEDS THE ANALYSIS. The covering / Mersenne structure lives not in the
    scalar r but in the per-prime INDEX-DIFFERENCE structure. For a prime with two
    representations (m1 > m2):
        2^{m1} + q1^{n1} = 2^{m2} + q2^{n2}
        => 2^{m2} * M_d = q2^{n2} - q1^{n1},   d = m1 - m2,  M_d = 2^d - 1.
    Every primitive factor ell of M_d (those with ord_ell(2) = d) is odd and divides
    the right side, giving q2^{n2} ≡ q1^{n1} (mod ell). This is the S-unit relation,
    per-prime, keyed on the index difference d. The graduated programme: k=2 gives one
    such constraint, k=3 gives three pairwise constraints that must be jointly
    consistent, and so on. The j-binning of (B) supplies the null/base measure to test
    whether the observed d's are biased toward small ord_ell(2).
    
    
    2026-06-27  mdiff_k2/k3 built (full census): index differences are parity-locked
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    
    Built primeparts.mdiff_k{2,3} over the full census (5,291,635,631 and
    3,332,361,926 rows = exact k_freq counts) + primeparts.mersenne_factors (full
    factorization of 2^d-1, d<=40). Per-k fixed-width: m_1..m_K sorted, d_i the
    canonical pairwise differences. Histogramming d confirms, at full scale, the
    parity result already seen in the covering-system triage:
    
      ALL index differences are EVEN. Odd d has single-digit counts across billions
      of primes (mdiff_k2.d_1: d=2 -> 2.4e8, d=4 -> 6.5e8, ..., d=12 -> 8.2e8 (mode,
      15.5%); but d=3 -> 7, d=5 -> 8, d=7 -> 4, d=9 -> 5). Same for all three k=3
      differences. Equivalently: within one prime every hit position m shares a
      common parity, fixed by p mod 3 -- ord_2(3)=2, so 3 | p-2^m on one parity
      class of m, killing it unless p-2^m is a literal power of 3. The handful of
      odd-d rows are exactly those power-of-3 exceptions. This holds across the
      whole range (not a small-p artifact); it is the mod-3 backbone imposing the
      sieve, the same {3,...} backbone the triage uses.
    
      The even-d mass tracks M_d small-factor richness: the mode d=12 is
      M_12 = 2^12-1 = 3^2.5.7.13 (the small primes with ord_2 in {2,3,4,12}, all
      dividing it); secondary peaks d=4 (3.5), 8 (3.5.17), 24. So d weights are
      biased toward small ord_ell(2), as conjectured -- the S-unit/covering signal.
    
    CONSEQUENCE FOR REPRESENTATION. Single-parity hit sets => store the hit set as
    one int64 bitmask (bit m set; m_max ~ 39 < 64, so this is k-agnostic, not just
    low k), drop the d-vector entirely (a deterministic bit-op on the mask) and
    prime_rank (= pi(p)). The mask factors as (anchor m_min, translation-invariant
    even-gap shape); the shape is low-cardinality (the d-distribution above), so
    dictionary+RLE on shape and delta on the anchor compress hard, and group-by-shape
    is itself the covering-pattern census.
    
      IMPLEMENTED. mdiff_k{K} now stores exactly (p, hit_mask int64); the m-vector
      and d-multiset are decoded on demand (HitMaskDiffs). The Mersenne-factor cache
      moved to its own builder (primeparts-mersenne -> mersenne_factors with ord2 +
      is_primitive, is_primitive = ord2==d). Replace is catalog-pure: a drop-purge
      through the catalog seam (no warehouse fs writes from the analysis tools).

    // ------------------------------------------------------------------ Stage L:
    // forced-q roots for q > Q
    
    struct LStat {
      uint64_t triples = 0, divisors = 0, hits = 0;
    };
    
    static void large_worker(std::atomic<int> &next, std::vector<LStat> &st,
                             std::atomic<int> &done) {
      fmpz_t N, r, q, P, R, T, A, p, two;
      fmpz_init(N);
      fmpz_init(r);
      fmpz_init(q);
      fmpz_init(P);
      fmpz_init(R);
      fmpz_init(T);
      fmpz_init(A);
      fmpz_init(p);
      fmpz_init(two);
      fmpz_set_ui(two, 2);
      const double log2Q = (double)cfg.qbits;
      for (;;) {
        int Dm = next.fetch_add(2);
        if (Dm > cfg.Mmax - 1)
          break;
        int k = Dm / 2;
        for (int m2 = 1; m2 <= k && m2 + Dm <= cfg.Mmax; ++m2) {
          int m1 = m2 + Dm;
          int n2lo =
              std::max(4, (3 * (m1 - 1)) / Dm + 1); // n1>=1, Dn>=3, q^3 < 2^Dm
          int n2hi = (int)std::floor(
              (m1 + 0.585) / log2Q); // q > Q  =>  n2 < (m1 + log2 1.5)/log2 Q
          if (n2hi < n2lo)
            continue;
          fmpz_one(N);
          fmpz_mul_2exp(N, N, m1);
          fmpz_one(T);
          fmpz_mul_2exp(T, T, m2);
          fmpz_sub(N, N, T); // N = 2^m1 - 2^m2
          for (int n2 = n2lo; n2 <= n2hi; ++n2) {
            st[Dm].triples++;
            (void)fmpz_root(r, N, n2); // floor root
            fmpz_add_ui(q, r, 1);      // the unique q with N < q^n2 <= 1.5N
            fmpz_pow_ui(P, q, n2);
            fmpz_sub(R, P, N); // must equal q^n1
            if (fmpz_cmp(R, q) >= 0) {
              slong e = fmpz_remove(T, R, q);
              if (e >= 1 && fmpz_is_one(T)) {
                st[Dm].hits++;
                fmpz_one(T);
                fmpz_mul_2exp(T, T, m2);
                fmpz_add(p, P, T);
                fmpz_one(A);
                fmpz_mul_2exp(A, A, Dm);
                fmpz_sub_ui(A, A, 1);
                fmpz_pow_ui(T, q, e);
                fmpz_divexact(A, A, T);
                record_hit("L", m1, m2, (int)e, n2, q, p, A);
              }
            }
            if (fmpz_is_odd(q)) { // structural note: does q | 2^Dm - 1 at all?
              fmpz_powm_ui(T, two, Dm, q);
              if (fmpz_is_one(T)) {
                st[Dm].divisors++;
                std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(g_mu);
                fmpz_sub_ui(T, q, 1);
                std::printf("  [L] Dm=%d m2=%d n2=%d: forced q (%lu bits) divides "
                            "2^Dm-1; v2(q-1)=%lu, prime=%d, exact=no\n",
                            Dm, m2, n2, (ulong)fmpz_bits(q), (ulong)fmpz_val2(T),
                            fmpz_is_probabprime(q));
              }
            }
          }
        }
        int d = done.fetch_add(1) + 1;
        if (d % 50 == 0)
          std::fprintf(stderr, "  stage L: %d even Dm done\n", d);
      }
      fmpz_clear(N);
      fmpz_clear(r);
      fmpz_clear(q);
      fmpz_clear(P);
      fmpz_clear(R);
      fmpz_clear(T);
      fmpz_clear(A);
      fmpz_clear(p);
      fmpz_clear(two);
      flint_cleanup();
    }

      fmpz_init(T);
      fmpz_init(Qn);

      fmpz_sub_ui(M, M, 1);
      fmpz_set_ui(qz, q);

      {

          break;

        if (c.m2 > k) {
          R.kill = K_M2;
          break;
        }

## Assistant

There is a useful deduction here before we choose a “factor rich versus factor poor” split. For q > 3, the closeness of the large terms forces:

```text
m₁ and m₂ even,
n₁ even,
n₂ odd.
```

This sharpens the situation considerably. The deductions below are additional to the original notes.

First, we already know q ≡ 1 modulo 3. Therefore:

```text
p = 2^m + q^n ≡ (−1)^m + 1 modulo 3.
```

Since p > 3 is prime, m must be even. Thus both m₁ and m₂ are even.

Now suppose n₂ were even. Then the two large terms would both be squares:

```text
q^n₂ − 2^m₁
    = [q^(n₂/2) − 2^(m₁/2)]
      [q^(n₂/2) + 2^(m₁/2)].
```

Their difference is positive because it equals q^n₁ − 2^m₂, and q > 2^m₂. Two distinct integer squares with the smaller root 2^(m₁/2) differ by at least:

```text
2·2^(m₁/2) + 1.
```

But our existing bound gives:

```text
q^n₁ − 2^m₂ ≤ 2^(M/2) + 1 − 2^m₂.
```

That is smaller, since m₁ = M+m₂. Contradiction. Hence n₂ is odd, and N odd then forces n₁ even.

So for q > 3 we now have:

```text
n₁ ≥ 2,
n₂ ≥ 5,
q² divides 2^M−1,
v₂(q−1) is even.
```

In particular, the n₂ = 4 branch we just discussed is excluded.

This strengthens your point (2). The exact coefficient relating the gap powers satisfies:

```text
2^m₂ / q^n₁ ≤ (q−1)/(3q²) < 1/(3q).
```

Consequently:

```text
q^N < (2^M−1)/(3q) + 1.
```

Along hypothetical solutions with q tending to infinity, the ratio q^N / 2^M actually tends to zero. The largest terms remain close, while the gap powers become increasingly unequal.

More importantly, **q² dividing the Mersenne number gives us a precise split to combine with Baker’s bound.**

Write:

```text
r = ord_q(2)
ρ = v_q(2^r−1).
```

The exact valuation identity is:

```text
n₁ = ρ + v_q(M).
```

Since n₁ is even, there are two substantially different ways the required square factor can arise.

- If ρ = 1, then v_q(M) must be odd and positive. In particular, q divides M.
- If q does not divide M, then ρ = n₁ must already be even and at least 2.

The second case says that q² already divides 2^r−1 at the first exponent r where q appears. This is a base-2 Wieferich condition. It is a specific arithmetic exception, rather than a vague assertion that the Mersenne number has few factors.

The branch **q divides M** gives exactly the kind of connection to the logarithmic bound we were missing. Because r also divides M and q does not divide r:

```text
q·r divides M.
```

Also q divides 2^r−1, so:

```text
r > log(q)/log(2).
```

Therefore:

```text
M > q·log(q)/log(2).
```

That lower bound can be compared with the explicit logarithmic inequality already in our notes, obtained from the [Laurent estimate quoted by MSS](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.18991v2#S6):

```text
M·log(2)/2
  < 25.2·log(q)²
      · max{log(3M/log(q)) + 0.38, 10}²
    + log(27/26).
```

**In this branch, the combination gives an absolute bound on q.** Using the conservative constants we already chose, q ≥ 1,000,000 is impossible.

The comparison can be made without guessing how M grows. Put t = M/log(q). Then t > q/log(2), while the logarithmic inequality gives:

```text
t / max{log(3t)+0.38, 10}² < 73·log(q).
```

For q ≥ 1,000,000, the left-hand expression is increasing throughout the relevant range of t. Substituting its lower endpoint therefore requires:

```text
q < 73·log(2)·log(q)·[log(q)+1.845126]².
```

At q = 1,000,000 the right side is below 172,000, and the discrepancy increases thereafter.

Thus the branch q | M has a finite reduction: q is bounded absolutely, and the existing logarithmic inequality then bounds M for each q. It has not yet been eliminated computationally.

Your proposed gaps M = 2s, with s an odd prime, fit especially neatly into the other branch. For q > 3:

```text
ord_q(2) is either s or 2s.
```

The possibilities 1 and 2 cannot occur. Hence:

```text
2s divides q−1,
q ≥ 2s+1 > M.
```

So q cannot divide M. We must therefore have:

```text
v_q(2^ord_q(2)−1) even and at least 2.
```

In other words, **a gap M = 2s can only survive through a repeated prime factor already present at q’s first appearance in the Mersenne sequence.**

That gives us a more controlled division of the problem:

```text
q divides M:
    the large factor q in M supplies a lower bound
    that combines with Baker to give a finite reduction.

q does not divide M:
    q must have an even first-occurrence valuation ≥ 2;
    this includes the possible M = 2s branches.
```

The second branch remains difficult. But this identifies a specific reason it escapes the first argument, and gives a sharper target than counting how many distinct factors 2^M−1 has.

    \subsection*{\S6. The common divisor $d = \gcd(\Delta m, \Delta n)$}
    
    The surviving space requires $\Delta m$ and $\Delta n$ coprime. This section records how far that requirement is proved. The letter $X$ is reserved above for the quadratic-form root $2^k q^j$; the block used here is written $Y$.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S6.1 Notation}
    
    Assume $d = \gcd(\Delta m, \Delta n) \geq 2$ and write
    \[
    \Delta m = c_1 d, \qquad \Delta n = c_2 d, \qquad \gcd(c_1,c_2) = 1,
    \]
    \[
    U = 2^{c_1} \ (\text{even}, \ \geq 2), \qquad V = q^{c_2} \ (\text{odd prime power}, \ \geq 3), \qquad Y = UV \geq 6 .
    \]
    Then $Y^d = 2^{\Delta m} q^{\Delta n}$, so the master identity reads
    \[
    A p = Y^d - 1 .
    \]
    Write $\Phi_e$ for the $e$-th cyclotomic polynomial, so that $Y^d - 1 = \prod_{e \mid d} \Phi_e(Y)$ with $\Phi_1(Y) = Y-1$.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S6.2 The bound on $A$}
    
    From the gap equations, $A < 2^{\Delta m}/q^{n_1}$ and $A < q^{\Delta n}/2^{m_2}$. Multiplying, with $m_2 \geq 1$, $n_1 \geq 1$, $q \geq 3$ giving $2^{m_2} q^{n_1} \geq 6$:
    \[
    A^2 < \frac{2^{\Delta m} q^{\Delta n}}{2^{m_2} q^{n_1}} \leq \frac{Y^d}{6},
    \qquad\text{so}\qquad
    \boxed{\,A < \frac{Y^{d/2}}{\sqrt 6}\,}
    \]
    
    \subsubsection*{\S6.3 Primality selects $\Phi_d$}
    
    The prime $p$ divides at least one factor $\Phi_e(Y)$ with $e \mid d$. Fix such an $e$; since $p \leq \Phi_e(Y)$,
    \[
    A = \frac{Y^d - 1}{p} \geq \frac{Y^d-1}{\Phi_e(Y)} .
    \]
    
    \emph{$e = 1$ is impossible.} It would give $A \geq \frac{Y^d-1}{Y-1} > Y^{d-1} \geq Y^{d/2}$ for $d \geq 2$, against \S6.2.
    
    \emph{$1 < e < d$ is impossible.} Such an $e$ satisfies $e \leq d/2$, and $\Phi_e(Y) \mid Y^e - 1 < Y^{d/2}$, so
    \[
    A > \frac{Y^d-1}{Y^{d/2}} = Y^{d/2} - Y^{-d/2} .
    \]
    Against \S6.2 this requires $\left(1 - 1/\sqrt6\right) Y^{d/2} < Y^{-d/2}$, i.e. $0.59\,Y^{d/2} < Y^{-d/2}$, false for $Y \geq 6$.
    
    Hence $p \mid \Phi_d(Y)$, with three consequences:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(C1)] $\displaystyle \prod_{e \mid d,\ e < d} \Phi_e(Y) = \frac{Y^d-1}{\Phi_d(Y)}$ divides $A$.
    \item[(C2)] $\operatorname{ord}_p(Y) = d$, since $p \nmid d$ and $p \nmid Y$; hence $p \equiv 1 \pmod d$.
    \item[(C3)] $\Phi_d(Y)/p$ is a positive integer, equal to $A \big/ \frac{Y^d-1}{\Phi_d(Y)}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    \subsubsection*{\S6.4 Every even $d$ is closed}
    
    For even $d$, $\Phi_d(Y)$ does not divide $Y^{d/2}-1$, so it divides the complementary factor:
    \[
    \Phi_d(Y) \ \Big| \ \frac{Y^d-1}{Y^{d/2}-1} = Y^{d/2}+1 .
    \]
    Therefore

    A \geq \frac{Y^d-1}{Y^{d/2}+1} = Y^{d/2}-1,
    \]
    contradicting \S6.2 by the computation above. At $d = 2$ this is $\Phi_2(Y) = Y+1$, recovering the difference-of-squares obstruction.

    (Y'-1) \mid U'^{\,3}-1, \qquad (Y'-1) \mid V'^{\,3}-1 .

    Modulo $Y'-1$ we have $U'V' \equiv 1$, so $V' \equiv U'^{-1}$ and the two divisibilities are a single condition. Write it for whichever of $U', V'$ is smaller, calling it $W$ and the other $Z$:
    \[
    W^2 \equiv Z \pmod{ZW-1}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad W^2 = i(ZW-1) + Z, \quad i \geq 0 .
    \]
    Since $W < Z$ we have $W^2 < ZW$. If $i \geq 1$ the right side is at least $ZW - 1 + Z > ZW$, a contradiction. So $i = 0$ and $W^2 = Z$, meaning $2^{2a} = q^{b}$ or $q^{2b} = 2^{a}$, impossible for distinct prime bases.
    
    With \S6.5, every $d$ divisible by $3$ is closed.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S6.7 $r$ prime, $r \geq 5$}
    
    The congruence of \S6.6 becomes $W^{r-1} \equiv Z \pmod{ZW-1}$, so
    \[
    Z = \frac{W^{r-1}+i}{iW+1}, \qquad i \geq 0 .
    \]
    Multiplying the numerator by $i^{r-1}$ and reducing modulo $iW+1$, where $iW \equiv -1$ and $r-1$ is even, gives $i^{r-1}\left(W^{r-1}+i\right) \equiv 1 + i^{r}$, hence
    \[
    (iW+1) \mid \left(i^{r}+1\right).
    \]
    Three regimes:
    \begin{itemize}
    \item $i = 0$ gives $Z = W^{r-1}$, impossible on distinct prime bases.
    \item $i = 1$ requires $(W+1) \mid \left(W^{r-1}+1\right)$. Since $W \equiv -1 \pmod{W+1}$ with $r-1$ even, $W^{r-1} \equiv 1$, so this needs $(W+1) \mid 2$. No solutions. The parametric family present at even exponents does not exist here.
    \item $i \geq 2$ is the live regime, bounded only weakly: $W \leq i^{r-1}$ from the divisibility, and $i \lesssim W^{r-3}$ from $Z > W$.
    \end{itemize}
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textbf{Where the $r=3$ argument stops.} The contradiction in \S6.6 needs $W^{r-1} \leq ZW$, that is
    \[
    Z \geq W^{r-2} .
    \]
    At $r=3$ this reads $Z \geq W$, true by construction. At $r \geq 5$ it is an additional hypothesis, and every pair with $W < Z < W^{r-2}$ escapes. The escape band widens with $r$.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textbf{Order reformulation.} Put $N = Y'-1 = 2^{a}q^{b}-1$, coprime to $q$ since $N \equiv -1 \pmod q$. By (C1), $N \mid A$, and $A q^{n_1} = 2^{ar}-1$, so
    \[
    \boxed{\,N = 2^{a}q^{b}-1 \ \text{ divides } \ 2^{ar}-1\,}
    \]
    Thus $\operatorname{ord}_N(2^{a}) \mid r$. It is not $1$, since $N \mid 2^a-1$ would force $N \leq 2^a - 1 < N$. As $r$ is prime, $\operatorname{ord}_N(2^{a}) = r$ exactly, and symmetrically $\operatorname{ord}_N(q^{b}) = r$. Consequently, for each prime $\ell \mid N$,
    \[
    \ell \mid 2^{a}-1 \qquad\text{or}\qquad \ell \equiv 1 \pmod r,
    \]
    with at least one $\ell$ of the second kind.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S6.8 Specialization to $\Delta m$ even, $\Delta n$ odd}
    
    Here $d$ is odd, so $c_2$ and $b$ are odd, while $c_1$ and $a$ are even --- so $U' = 2^{a}$ is a perfect square. By \S6.6 every prime factor of $d$ is at least $5$. Carried in from \S5: $m_2 = v_2(q-1)$, $n_1 = v_q\!\left(2^{\Delta m}-1\right)$, and $A$ is the $q$-free part of $2^{\Delta m}-1$.
    
    Two conditions on the primes of $N$ arrive from different directions and hold simultaneously:
    \begin{itemize}
    \item From \S6.7: every prime $\ell \mid N$ divides $2^{a}-1$ or satisfies $\ell \equiv 1 \pmod r$.
    \item From \S5.4: $N \mid 2^{\Delta m}-1$ and $\Delta n$ is odd, so every prime $\ell \mid N$ with $\ell \neq q$ has $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$ odd, hence $\left(\frac{q}{\ell}\right) = 1$.
    \end{itemize}
    Alongside these, (C2) gives $p \equiv 1 \pmod r$, and (C3) caps the cofactor $\Phi_r(Y')/p$ below roughly $Y'^{\,r/2-1}/\sqrt6$, forcing $p$ to be a nearly full-size factor of $\Phi_r(Y')$ while $\operatorname{ord}_p(Y') = r$.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S6.9 The congruence modulo $V'+1$}
    
    Take the divisibility of \S6.6 in the form that solves for $U'$:
    \[
    V'^{\,r-1} - U' = t\left(U'V'-1\right), \qquad t \geq 0 .
    \]
    Since $U' < U'V'-1$, $U'$ is the least positive residue of $V'^{\,r-1}$ modulo $U'V'-1$, so $t \geq 0$; and $t = 0$ would give $U' = V'^{\,r-1}$, impossible on distinct prime bases. Hence $t \geq 1$ and
    \[
    U' = \frac{V'^{\,r-1}+t}{tV'+1} .
    \]
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textbf{$t$ is odd.} Were $t$ even, both $V'^{\,r-1}+t$ and $tV'+1$ would be odd, making $U'$ odd; but $U' = 2^{a}$ with $a \geq 1$.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textbf{The congruence.} Reduce $U'\left(tV'+1\right) = V'^{\,r-1}+t$ modulo $V'+1$, where $V' \equiv -1$ and $r-1$ is even:
    \[
    \boxed{\,U'(1-t) \equiv 1+t \pmod{V'+1}\,}
    \]
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textbf{The $2$-adic split.} By \S6.8 the exponent $b$ is odd, so lifting the exponent gives $v_2(V'-1) = v_2(q-1) = m_2$. For $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $m_2 \geq 2$, hence $V' \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and
    \[
    v_2(V'+1) = 1, \qquad V'+1 = 2w \quad\text{with } w \text{ odd},\ w \geq 3 .
    \]
    Modulo $2$ the congruence holds identically, since $U'$ is even and $t$ is odd. Setting $\alpha = (t-1)/2$ and $\beta = (t+1)/2$, so that $\beta = \alpha+1$ and $\gcd(\alpha,\beta) = 1$, division by $2$ gives
    \[
    U'\alpha \equiv -\beta \pmod{w} .
    \]
    
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(P1)] $\gcd\!\left(\frac{t-1}{2},\ \frac{V'+1}{2}\right) = 1$. A common prime would divide $\beta$, against $\gcd(\alpha,\beta) = 1$.
    \item[(P2)] $\alpha$ is invertible modulo $w$, so
    \[
    U' \equiv -\frac{t+1}{t-1} \pmod{w} .
    \]
    \item[(P3)] Since $U' = 2^{a}$, this class lies in $\langle 2 \rangle \subseteq \left(\mathbb{Z}/w\mathbb{Z}\right)^\times$, of index $\varphi(w)/\operatorname{ord}_w(2)$.
    \item[(P4)] By \S6.8 the exponent $a$ is even, so $U'$ is a perfect square. Since
    \[
    -\frac{t+1}{t-1} = \frac{1-t^2}{(t-1)^2}
    \]
    with $(t-1)^2$ a unit square modulo $w$ by (P1), every prime $\ell \mid w$ satisfies
    \[
    \left(\frac{1-t^{2}}{\ell}\right) = 1 .
    \]
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Because $b$ is odd, $q+1$ divides $q^{b}+1$, and $v_2(q+1) = 1$ for $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so $(q+1)/2$ is an odd divisor of $w$. Hence $1-t^{2}$ is a quadratic residue modulo every prime dividing $(q+1)/2$, independent of $b$.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textbf{The symmetric side.} Writing $U'^{\,r-1} - V' = s\left(U'V'-1\right)$ and reducing $V'\left(sU'+1\right) = U'^{\,r-1}+s$ modulo the odd number $U'+1$ gives $s$ odd together with
    \[
    \gcd\!\left(\frac{s-1}{2},\ U'+1\right) = 1, \qquad V' \equiv -\frac{s+1}{s-1} \pmod{2^{a}+1} .
    \]
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textbf{Scope.} The split uses $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. For $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, $m_2 = 1$, so $V' \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and $v_2(V'+1) \geq 2$; that sub-branch needs separate treatment.
    
    \medskip
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{ll}
    \hline
    $d = \gcd(\Delta m, \Delta n)$ & status \\
    \hline
    even & closed, \S6.4 \\
    odd, divisible by $3$ & closed, \S6.5 then \S6.6 \\
    odd, least prime factor $\geq 5$ & open, \S6.7 \\
    \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    
    \subsection*{\S7. The parity of $n_1$}
    
    \subsubsection*{\S7.1 Both parities are fixed wherever \S4 speaks}
    
    $\Delta n$ odd makes $n_1$ and $n_2$ of opposite parity, so the $n_2$ column of \S4 determines $n_1$ as well:
    \[
    q \equiv 3 \!\!\pmod 8 \ \Rightarrow\ n_2 \text{ even},\ n_1 \text{ odd}; \qquad
    q \equiv 7 \!\!\pmod 8 \ \Rightarrow\ n_2 \text{ odd},\ n_1 \text{ even}.
    \]
    For $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ the Legendre condition is already satisfied by \S5.2, so it fixes neither parity.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S7.2 $q \equiv 7 \pmod 8$ forces a square divisor}
    
    Here $n_1$ is even with $n_1 \geq 1$, hence $n_1 \geq 2$, hence
    \[
    \boxed{\,q^{2} \mid 2^{\Delta m}-1, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \operatorname{ord}_{q^{2}}(2) \mid \Delta m\,}
    \]
    Since $\operatorname{ord}_{q^2}(2)$ equals $\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$ or $q\cdot\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$, reading this as $q \mid \Delta m$ would require $q$ to be non-Wieferich for base $2$. Stated as the divisibility above it carries no such hypothesis.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S7.3 The parity condition on $v_q(\Delta m)$}
    
    By \S5.6, with $e = \operatorname{ord}_q(2)$,
    \[
    n_1 = v_q\!\left(2^{\Delta m}-1\right) = v_q\!\left(2^{e}-1\right) + v_q(\Delta m),
    \]
    so \S7.1 becomes a congruence on $v_q(\Delta m)$ modulo $2$. For $q = 3$, where $e = 2$ and $v_3\!\left(2^2-1\right) = 1$, this reads $n_1 = 1 + v_3(\Delta m)$, and $3 \equiv 3 \pmod 8$ requires $n_1$ odd, so
    \[
    v_3(\Delta m) \text{ is even},
    \]
    removing $\Delta m = 6, 12, 24, 30, 48, \dots$ from the $q = 3$ branch.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S7.4 A perfect square}
    
    Exactly one of $n_1, n_2$ is even, so exactly one of $q^{n_1}, q^{n_2}$ is a perfect square, hence exactly one of $p - 2^{m_1}$, $p - 2^{m_2}$ is. Since $2^{m_2}$ is fixed by $q$ through \S5.2:
    \[
    q \equiv 3 \!\!\pmod 8: \quad p - 2 = \left(q^{n_2/2}\right)^{2}, \qquad
    q \equiv 7 \!\!\pmod 8: \quad p - 2^{m_1} = \left(q^{n_1/2}\right)^{2}.
    \]
    In the first case $q^{n_2/2}$ is odd, so $p \equiv 3 \pmod 8$. The statement is unconditional, but silent for $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where \S4 leaves the parity of $n_2$ free.
    
    \subsubsection*{\S7.5 Where the branches stand}
    
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tabular}{lll}
    \hline
    $q \bmod 8$ & $m_2$ & available from \S4 \\
    \hline
    $3$ & $1$ & $n_1$ odd; $p - 2$ a perfect square \\
    $7$ & $1$ & $n_1$ even, so $\operatorname{ord}_{q^2}(2) \mid \Delta m$; $p - 2^{m_1}$ a perfect square \\
    $5$ & $2$ & symbol automatic --- no parity information \\
    $1$ & $v_2(q-1) \geq 3$ & symbol automatic --- no parity information \\
    \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \end{center}
    
    \subsection*{\S8. The factorization $A = u\Psi$}
    $2^M-1=Aq^{n_1}$ gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:valuation-coupling}
    \boxed{
    v_\ell(2^{d_\ell}-1)+v_\ell(M)
     =v_\ell(q-1)+v_\ell(N).}
    \end{equation}
    Here $\ell\nmid d_\ell$ because $d_\ell\mid\ell-1$, and $\ell\neq q$.
    For example, if $q\neq3$, then $3\mid q-1$ and
    \[
    1+v_3(M)=v_3(q-1)+v_3(N).
    \]
    Thus the order conditions and the multiplicity conditions constrain
    the same two gaps.
    
    \subsection*{Quadratic reciprocity and the parity of $n_1$}
    
    We already know $(q/p)=1$. Also
    \[
    \left(\frac pq\right)=\left(\frac2q\right)^{m_2}.

    \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
    q\bmod8&m_2&n_1&n_2\\ \hline
    3&1&\text{odd}&\text{even}\\
    7&1&\text{even}&\text{odd}\\
    5&2&\multicolumn{2}{c}{\text{opposite parities; neither specified}}\\
    1&v_2(q-1)\geq3&\multicolumn{2}{c}{\text{opposite parities; neither specified}}
    \end{array}
    \]

    It does not by itself force $q\mid M$.
    More generally, with $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-q-valuation}
    n_1=v_q(2^r-1)+v_q(M).
    \end{equation}
    This follows from lifting the exponent, since $r\mid M$ and $q\nmid r$.
    The parity of the right side is therefore specified in the first two
    rows of the table, without any Wieferich assumption.

The additional argument gives, for q > 3:

But both q ≡ 3 and q ≡ 7 modulo 8 require m₂ = 1. Hence both disappear. We are left with:

q ≡ 1 modulo 8:  m₂ even and at least 4

In both remaining cases, the difference-of-squares argument gives n₁ even and n₂ odd. The prime q = 3 remains separate: it has m₂ = 1, n₁ odd, and n₂ even.

On §6, I agree that I gave it too little weight. I focused on the unfinished claim that the gaps are coprime, but the section provides useful restrictions even without proving that claim.

Its main construction is this. If an odd prime s divides both M and N, put:

V = q^(N/s)
B = U·V − 1.

B divides 2^M−1,
B divides q^N−1.

So an assumed common factor of the gaps forces a **particular structured divisor** into A. We are no longer merely asking which arbitrary factors the Mersenne number might have.

The cyclotomic argument also locates p in the remaining factor and gives:

The s = 3 argument is a completed exclusion. For s ≥ 5, the divisibility conditions remain useful even though the section does not reach a contradiction.

There is a particularly relevant consequence of the new parity reduction: **the q ≡ 1 modulo 4 hypothesis in §6.9 now holds throughout the q > 3 branch.** That section’s congruence modulo V+1, its subgroup condition, and its square-residue condition therefore apply to every remaining q > 3 case with a common prime divisor of M and N. There is also a useful limit on where §6 applies. For the proposed family M = 2s with s an odd prime and q > 3, we found:

## Assistant

**The q = 3 branch can be closed entirely with the elementary conditions already in the notes.** We do not need Baker’s estimate here.

We have:

```text
m₂ = 1,
M even,
N odd,

A·3^n₁ = 2^M−1,
2A = 3^N−1.
```

Lifting the exponent gives:

```text
n₁ = v₃(2^M−1) = 1 + v₃(M).
```

Suppose n₁ > 1. Then 3 divides M. Since the order of 2 modulo 7 is 3:

```text
7 divides 2^M−1.
```

The factor 7 cannot belong to 3^n₁, so it divides A. The other gap equation then requires:

```text
7 divides 3^N−1.
```

But the order of 3 modulo 7 is 6. Therefore 6 divides N, contradicting N odd.

Thus:

```text
n₁ = 1.
```

Now the two representations become:

```text
p = 2^m₁ + 3 = 2 + 3^n₂,
```

so:

```text
3^n₂ − 1 = 2^m₁.
```

Since n₂ = n₁+N is even, factor:

```text
[3^(n₂/2)−1] · [3^(n₂/2)+1] = 2^m₁.
```

Both factors are powers of 2 and differ by 2. They must therefore be 2 and 4. This gives:

```text
n₂ = 2,
m₁ = 3,
p = 11.
```

So q = 3 has no A > 1 solution.

The useful mechanism is very specific: **increasing the multiplicity of 3 in the Mersenne number requires 3 | M; that forces the additional Mersenne factor 7, whose order condition contradicts N odd.**

For general q, the corresponding step would be to exploit q | M to force another factor of 2^M−1 whose order at base q is incompatible with N. For q = 3, the factor 7 supplies that contradiction immediately.

    $2^M-1=Aq^{n_1}$ gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:valuation-coupling}
    \boxed{
    v_\ell(2^{d_\ell}-1)+v_\ell(M)
     =v_\ell(q-1)+v_\ell(N).}
    \end{equation}
    Here $\ell\nmid d_\ell$ because $d_\ell\mid\ell-1$, and $\ell\neq q$.
    For example, if $q\neq3$, then $3\mid q-1$ and
    \[
    1+v_3(M)=v_3(q-1)+v_3(N).
    \]
    Thus the order conditions and the multiplicity conditions constrain
    the same two gaps.
    
    \subsection*{Quadratic reciprocity and the parity of $n_1$}
    
    We already know $(q/p)=1$. Also
    \[
    \left(\frac pq\right)=\left(\frac2q\right)^{m_2}.
    \]
    If $q\equiv1\pmod4$, reciprocity and
    $m_2=v_2(q-1)$ make $(q/p)=1$ automatic: for $q\equiv1\pmod8$
    we have $(2/q)=1$, and for $q\equiv5\pmod8$ we have $m_2=2$.
    If $q\equiv3\pmod4$, then $m_2=1$ and
    $p\equiv2+(-1)^{n_2}\pmod4$. Reciprocity therefore gives
    \[
    \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
    q\bmod8&m_2&n_1&n_2\\ \hline
    3&1&\text{odd}&\text{even}\\
    7&1&\text{even}&\text{odd}\\
    5&2&\multicolumn{2}{c}{\text{opposite parities; neither specified}}\\
    1&v_2(q-1)\geq3&\multicolumn{2}{c}{\text{opposite parities; neither specified}}
    \end{array}
    \]
    In particular $q\equiv7\pmod8$ forces $q^2\mid2^M-1$.
    It does not by itself force $q\mid M$.
    More generally, with $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-q-valuation}
    n_1=v_q(2^r-1)+v_q(M).
    \end{equation}
    This follows from lifting the exponent, since $r\mid M$ and $q\nmid r$.
    The parity of the right side is therefore specified in the first two
    rows of the table, without any Wieferich assumption.
    
    \subsection*{Additional results already in the second document}
    
    These are supporting facts, separate from the main chain above.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textit{A completed family exclusion.}
    If $M=2k$ and $q=2^k-1$ is prime with $k\geq3$, then
    \[
    n_1=1,\qquad A=2^k+1,\qquad m_2=1.
    \]
    Hence $q^N=2^{k+1}+3$. It fails for $N=1$, while for $N\geq3$,
    \[
    (2^k-1)^3>2^{k+1}+3.
    \]
    For example, writing $x=2^k\geq8$, the difference is
    $x^3-3x^2+x-4>0$.
    Thus this family is excluded. There is no proof that all remaining
    possibilities belong to this family. In particular the size interval
    alone does not put $N$ strictly below $2$ in this family; its upper
    endpoint is slightly larger than $2$.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textit{A common factor of $3$ is excluded.}
    Suppose $3\mid M,N$, and put $U=2^{M/3}$, $V=q^{N/3}$.
    Lemma~\ref{lem:divisor} gives $UV-1\mid A$, so
    $UV-1\mid U^3-1,V^3-1$.
    Let $W=\min(U,V)$ and $Z=\max(U,V)$; $W<Z$ since their prime bases
    differ. Multiplication by $Z$ modulo $WZ-1$ gives
    \[
    W^2\equiv Z\pmod{WZ-1}.
    \]
    Both $W^2$ and $Z$ lie strictly between $0$ and $WZ-1$, so $W^2=Z$,
    impossible for powers of distinct primes.
    Thus $3\nmid\gcd(M,N)$. This does not prove $\gcd(M,N)=1$;
    the discussion of higher odd common factors in the original is deferred.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textit{Primitive prime divisors (external input used in the original).}
    Using Zsigmondy's theorem, as the second document does, $q^N-1$ with
    $N\geq3$ odd has a prime divisor $\ell_0$ with
    \[
    \operatorname{ord}_{\ell_0}(q)=N,\qquad
    \ell_0\mid\Psi\mid2^M-1,\qquad
    \ell_0\equiv1\pmod{2N}.
    \]
    This uses the primitive-divisor theorem, not just the elementary order
    argument; a reference for that theorem should be supplied before treating
    these notes as self-contained.
    Similarly, for fixed $(q,N)$, a primitive divisor of $2^M-1$ gives
    \[
    M\in\{\operatorname{ord}_P(2): P\text{ prime},\ P\mid q(q^N-1)\}
     \cup\{6\}.
    \]
    Here $M\geq6$ is even, and $6$ is the only relevant exceptional exponent.
    This is a finiteness statement for fixed $(q,N)$, not a global bound.

    \section*{Additional work: application and adaptation of Miyazaki--Scott--Styer}
    
    \noindent\textit{Provenance and priority.}
    Everything in this block is additional to the two original notes.
    Statements from Miyazaki--Scott--Styer (MSS) are identified explicitly;
    the applications and calculations below were made while consolidating
    these notes. They are not attributed to the original notes or claimed
    as new results in the literature.
    Priority is: first the logarithmic inequality, then the polynomial
    adaptation, then the determinant conditions. An absolute bound on $q$
    is still missing. All statements continue to assume the prime solution.
    
    \subsection*{What applies from MSS, and what does not}
    
    The system is a special case of $a^x+b^y=c^z$ with
    $(a,b,c)=(2,q,p)$ and $z=Z=1$. MSS's complete results for
    $c=7,13,97$ exclude those values of $p$ here. Their more general effective
    results fix $c$ in specified families, so a bound depending on $c=p$
    does not supply a global bound for our problem. Their Pillai theorem
    concerns a difference of powers and is not directly a theorem about
    our sum. See the theorem statements and outline in \cite{MSS}.
    
    Their polynomial-exponential equation matches our equality exactly:
    \[
    X^a-X^b=q^{y_1}-q^{y_2},\qquad
    (X,a,b,y_1,y_2)=(2,m_1,m_2,n_2,n_1).
    \]
    But the proposition labeled \texttt{prop-EuAl} in the local MSS source
    assumes $(a-b)/E$ odd, where $E$ is the least positive exponent for which
    $X^E\equiv\pm1\pmod q$. This is a signed order, unlike our ordinary orders.
    For $X=2$ put $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$. If $r$ is odd, $E=r$,
    and $M/E$ is even. If $r$ is even, $E=r/2$, and $M/E=2(M/r)$ is even.
    Thus the proposition as stated never applies to this specialization.
    The polynomial argument below is a separate adaptation, not an invocation
    of that proposition.
    
    \subsection*{First priority: an explicit logarithmic inequality}
    
    \noindent\textit{Additional deduction, proved here using the consolidated bounds.}
    Define
    \[
    \Lambda=n_2\log q-m_1\log2.
    \]
    The subtracted equation yields
    \[
    2^{m_1}(1-2^{-M})=q^{n_2}(1-q^{-N}),
    \]
    hence
    \[
    \Lambda=\log(1-2^{-M})-\log(1-q^{-N}).
    \]
    Since $q^N<2^M$ and $q^N\geq27$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:lambda-upper}
    \boxed{0<\Lambda<\frac{27}{26}q^{-N}.}
    \end{equation}
    Indeed, $-\log(1-x)\leq x/(1-x)$ for $0<x<1$.
    In particular the linear form is nonzero.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textit{External input: Laurent's estimate quoted by MSS.}
    The proposition labeled \texttt{prop-comp} in MSS gives
    \[
    \log|b_2\log\alpha_2-b_1\log\alpha_1|
    >-25.2H_1H_2\bigl(\max\{\log b'+0.38,10\}\bigr)^2,
    \qquad b'=b_1/H_2+b_2/H_1,
    \]
    under its height and independence hypotheses.
    Use $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(2,q)$, $(b_1,b_2)=(m_1,n_2)$.
    The bases are multiplicatively independent because they are distinct primes.
    For a conservative application choose $H_1=H_2=\log q>1$;
    these dominate both rational heights, both logarithms, and $1$.
    This choice also avoids any issue with the mismatched index in the height
    condition printed in the local copy. Sharper admissible heights could
    improve the constants, but are not needed for the deduction below.
    
    Put $\lambda=\log q$ and
    \[
    \mathcal H=\max\left\{\log\frac{m_1+n_2}{\lambda}+0.38,10\right\}.
    \]
    Combining the quoted lower bound with \eqref{eq:lambda-upper} gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:baker-gap}
    N\lambda<25.2\lambda^2\mathcal H^2+\log(27/26).
    \end{equation}
    
    The dependence on $m_1,n_2$ can be removed in favor of $M,q$.
    Since $m_2\leq M/2$, $m_1\leq3M/2$. Also
    $q^{n_2}<p<2^{m_1+1}$, so
    \[
    n_2<\frac{(3M/2+1)\log2}{\lambda}.
    \]
    Since $\lambda\geq\log3$, $\log2/\log3<2/3$, and $M\geq6$,
    these inequalities give $m_1+n_2<3M$.
    Together with $N\lambda>M\log2/2$, this proves
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:baker-M}
    \boxed{
    \frac{M\log2}{2}
    <25.2(\log q)^2
    \left(\max\left\{\log\frac{3M}{\log q}+0.38,10\right\}\right)^2
    +\log(27/26).}
    \end{equation}
    
    \noindent\textit{What this establishes.}
    For each fixed $q$, the right side grows like $(\log M)^2$ whereas the
    left side grows like $M$. It therefore gives an effective upper bound
    on $M$ for that fixed $q$, and then bounds all four exponents by the
    consolidated identities and bounds. This is an actual consequence of the
    quoted logarithmic estimate, not a proposed conclusion.
    It does not bound $q$ absolutely. No finite computation over all $q$ has
    yet been justified.
    
    \noindent\textit{Next question.}
    Can the order and valuation conditions force a lower bound on $M$ in terms
    of $q$ incompatible with \eqref{eq:baker-M}? The existing bound
    $q<2^{M/3}$ only gives $M>3\log q/\log2$, which is not enough by itself.
    The proposed combination remains open.
    
    \subsection*{Second priority: a polynomial identity allowing either parity}
    
    \noindent\textit{Additional calculation inspired by MSS; proved below.}
    Use the ordinary order and write
    \[
    r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2),\qquad M=rh,\qquad
    \eta=v_q(h),\qquad \rho=v_q(2^r-1).
    \]
    Here $r\geq2$, $q\nmid r$, $\rho\geq1$, and
    $n_1=\rho+\eta$ by lifting the exponent.
    The letter $u$ remains the odd part of $q-1$; it is not used for this
    valuation.
    Define
    \[
    F_r(t)=\frac{t^r-1}{t-1},\qquad
    J_h(t)=1+t^r+\cdots+t^{r(h-1)},\qquad
    G(t)=t^{m_2}(t-1)J_h(t).
    \]
    We have
    \[
    F_r(2)=2^r-1,\qquad
    F_r(2)G(2)=q^{n_1}(q^N-1).
    \]
    The polynomial identity below does not require $h$ odd.
    
    Put
    \[
    H_r(t)=\frac{F_r(t)-r}{t-1}\in\mathbb Z[t],
    \qquad c\in\{0,\ldots,r-1\},\quad c\equiv-m_2\pmod r,
    \]
    and let $R(t)$ be the remainder of $-t^cH_r(t)$ on division by the
    monic polynomial $F_r(t)$. Then there is $P(t)\in\mathbb Z[t]$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:adapted-bezout}
    \boxed{F_r(t)P(t)+G(t)R(t)=rh=M.}
    \end{equation}
    To check this, work modulo $F_r(t)$. We have $t^r\equiv1$,
    $J_h(t)\equiv h$, and $(t-1)H_r(t)\equiv-r$. Therefore
    \[
    G(t)R(t)\equiv
    -h t^{m_2+c}(t-1)H_r(t)\equiv rh.
    \]
    Since $F_r$ is monic, the quotient defining $P$ has integer coefficients.
    
    Evaluate \eqref{eq:adapted-bezout} at $2$ and multiply by $F_r(2)$.
    Using the original equation gives the exact identity
    \[
    q^{n_1}R(2)+M(2^r-1)
    =(2^r-1)^2P(2)+q^{n_2}R(2).
    \]
    Consequently
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:adapted-congruence}
    \boxed{
    q^{n_1}R(2)+M(2^r-1)
    \equiv0\pmod{q^{\min\{2\rho,n_2\}}}.}
    \end{equation}
    This supplies an even-quotient version of the type of congruence used
    by MSS, with an explicitly stated modulus and no unverified size hypothesis.
    
    \medskip
    \noindent\textit{How much information does it give?}
    Write $h=q^\eta h_0$ and $2^r-1=q^\rho K$ with $q\nmid h_0K$.
    If $\rho>\eta$, division by $q^{n_1}$ gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:adapted-divided}
    \boxed{R(2)+r h_0K\equiv0\pmod{q^{\min\{\rho-\eta,N\}}}.}
    \end{equation}
    If $\eta\geq\rho$, the modulus in
    \eqref{eq:adapted-congruence} is at most $q^{n_1}$, and both left-hand
    terms are already divisible by that modulus. It then adds no restriction.
    In particular, when $\rho=1$ the calculation gives new restrictions
    only if $\eta=0$, and then only modulo $q$.
    There is no claim here that this improves on all elementary expansions
    of the original equation.
    
    For orientation, $r=2$ gives $q=3$ and $R(t)=1$, since $m_2=1$.
    If $\eta=0$, \eqref{eq:adapted-divided} says $1+2h\equiv0\pmod3$,
    so $h\equiv1\pmod3$. This checks the formula in its smallest case;
    it does not settle the $q=3$ branch.
    
    \noindent\textit{Next question.}
    The identity is proved, but a useful global estimate is not.
    We would need control of the size and sign of $R(2)+r h_0K$, or a
    stronger modulus, sufficient to combine with \eqref{eq:baker-M}.
    The degree of $R$ can grow with $r$, so a large modulus alone does not
    supply that comparison. This is the same kind of size issue emphasized
    in MSS's closing discussion.
    
    \subsection*{Third priority: retain the information modulo $p$}
    
    \noindent\textit{Application of the determinant idea in MSS, proved here.}
    Set
    \[
    T=m_1n_2-m_2n_1=m_2N+Mn_1+MN>0.
    \]
    From $2^{m_i}\equiv-q^{n_i}\pmod p$, raising the two congruences
    to $n_2,n_1$ respectively and dividing gives
    \[
    2^T\equiv(-1)^{n_2-n_1}=-1\pmod p.
    \]
    Similarly, using exponents $m_1,m_2$ gives
    \[
    q^T\equiv(-1)^{m_1-m_2}=1\pmod p.
    \]
    Thus
    \[
    \operatorname{ord}_p(q)\mid T,\qquad
    \operatorname{ord}_p(2)\mid2T,\qquad
    \operatorname{ord}_p(2)\nmid T.
    \]
    These are necessary conditions involving the prime $p$ itself.
    They have not yet been combined into a new bound.
    The normalization of orders used elsewhere in MSS should not be assumed
    to preserve our fixed base $2$ without checking the change of variables.
    
    \subsection*{What remains open}
    
    The consolidated original material gives exact valuations, a size interval,
    order conditions, multiplicity identities, and some completed exclusions.
    The additional logarithmic calculation bounds the exponents for each
    fixed $q$. The additional polynomial calculation supplies a proved
    congruence with a precise limitation when $\eta\geq\rho$.
    None of these presently bounds $q$ absolutely or excludes every prime
    solution with $A>1$.
    
    The immediate priority is to determine whether their combination can
    bound $q$, or can exclude all sufficiently large $q$ in explicit branches.
    Only after such a finite reduction would a finite computation finish
    the whole problem. No search implementation is part of these notes.

        \noindent\textit{Consolidated from the original common-divisor section.}

        \[

        \subsection*{An effective reduction when $q\mid M$}
        
        \noindent\textit{Added in discussion; uses the quoted Laurent estimate.}
        If $q\mid M$, then $qr\mid M$ because $r\mid M$ and $q\nmid r$.
        Since $q<2^r$, this gives
        \[
        M\geq qr>\frac{q\log q}{\log2}.
        \]
        Together with \eqref{eq:baker-M}, this bounds $q$ absolutely in this branch.
        Here is a coarse explicit cutoff, retained for checking by hand.
        
        Put $\lambda=\log q$, $t=M/\lambda$, and
        $H(t)=\max\{\log(3t)+0.38,10\}$. Dividing \eqref{eq:baker-M} gives
        \[
        \frac{t}{H(t)^2}
         <\frac{50.4}{\log2}\lambda
           +\frac{2\log(27/26)}{\lambda\log2\,H(t)^2}
         <73\lambda.
        \]
        If $q\geq10^6$, then $t>q/\log2$, $H(t)=\log(3t)+0.38>2$,
        and $t/H(t)^2$ is increasing. Hence
        \[
        q<73\log2\,\lambda(\lambda+C)^2,
        \qquad C=\log(3/\log2)+0.38<1.845126.
        \]
        At $q=10^6$ the right side is less than $172000$.
        Moreover $q/[\log q(\log q+C)^2]$ is increasing thereafter:
        its logarithmic derivative with respect to $\lambda$ is
        $1-1/\lambda-2/(\lambda+C)>0$.
        Thus $q<10^6$ in this branch. For each such $q$,
        \eqref{eq:baker-M} bounds $M$ effectively. This is a finite reduction,
        not an elimination of the branch; no final computation has been performed.

    \begin{lemma}\label{lem:qthree}

    we get $7\mid2^M-1$, hence $7\mid A$, hence $7\mid3^N-1$.
    But $\operatorname{ord}_7(3)=6$, contradicting $N$ odd.

    \[
    3^{n_2}-1=2^{m_1},\qquad n_2=1+N\text{ even}.

    The factors $3^{n_2/2}-1$ and $3^{n_2/2}+1$ are powers of $2$
    differing by $2$, so they are $2$ and $4$. Thus $n_2=2$, $m_1=3$,
    and $p=11$, which has $A=1$.

    \subsection*{An effective reduction when $q\mid M$}
    
    \noindent\textit{Added in discussion; uses the quoted Laurent estimate.}
    If $q\mid M$, then $qr\mid M$ because $r\mid M$ and $q\nmid r$.
    Since $q<2^r$, this gives
    \[
    M\geq qr>\frac{q\log q}{\log2}.
    \]
    Together with \eqref{eq:baker-M}, this bounds $q$ absolutely in this branch.
    Here is a coarse explicit cutoff, retained for checking by hand.
    
    Put $\lambda=\log q$, $t=M/\lambda$, and
    $H(t)=\max\{\log(3t)+0.38,10\}$. Dividing \eqref{eq:baker-M} gives
    \[
    \frac{t}{H(t)^2}
     <\frac{50.4}{\log2}\lambda
       +\frac{2\log(27/26)}{\lambda\log2\,H(t)^2}
     <73\lambda.
    \]
    If $q\geq10^6$, then $t>q/\log2$, $H(t)=\log(3t)+0.38>2$,
    and $t/H(t)^2$ is increasing. Hence
    \[
    q<73\log2\,\lambda(\lambda+C)^2,
    \qquad C=\log(3/\log2)+0.38<1.845126.
    \]
    At $q=10^6$ the right side is less than $172000$.
    Moreover $q/[\log q(\log q+C)^2]$ is increasing thereafter:
    its logarithmic derivative with respect to $\lambda$ is
    $1-1/\lambda-2/(\lambda+C)>0$.
    Thus $q<10^6$ in this branch. For each such $q$,
    \eqref{eq:baker-M} bounds $M$ effectively. This is a finite reduction,
    not an elimination of the branch; no final computation has been performed.
